#### F3_semantic_groups_table
# CLCA Protocol v3.2 — F3 SEMANTIC GROUPS TABLE
# Language: English (en)

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|-------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| GROUP 1: CORRESPONDENCE TO FACTS | Terms used to evaluate whether statements, beliefs, or representations correspond to actual facts or reality. These expressions are primarily applied to propositions, claims, and assertions, marking whether they accurately describe the world. Commonly used in contexts of verification, fact-checking, and epistemic evaluation. | **Core:** true, false, correct, incorrect, right, wrong, accurate, inaccurate, erroneous<br>**Constructions:** the truth of the matter, get it right/wrong, prove false, hold true | **true/truth** spans GROUP 1, 10, 3; **false/falsity** spans GROUP 1, 2, 11; **correct/incorrect** spans GROUP 1, 10, 9; **right/wrong** spans GROUP 1, 10 | Focus on propositional content rather than objects or persons. Regularly contrasted in verification contexts. |
| GROUP 2: AUTHENTICITY OF OBJECTS AND CREDENTIALS | Terms used to distinguish genuine articles, documents, or credentials from counterfeits, imitations, or fraudulent versions. These expressions evaluate whether physical objects, artworks, documents, or credentials are what they purport to be, focusing on origin, authorship, and legitimacy rather than abstract truth. Common in commercial, legal, and art contexts. | **Core:** genuine, authentic, fake, counterfeit, bogus, spurious<br>**Constructions:** the genuine article, the real McCoy, the real deal, fake it till you make it, spot a fake, under false pretenses<br>**Derivations:** authenticate, authentication, counterfeit (verb), fakery | **false/falsity** overlaps from GROUP 1; **real/reality** overlaps from GROUP 3; **bogus** shows limited integration | Apply to tangible objects and documents rather than abstract propositions. |
| GROUP 3: ONTOLOGICAL REALITY VS. APPEARANCE | Terms that distinguish actual existence or substance from appearance, simulation, imagination, or virtuality. These expressions mark whether something exists in the physical/actual world versus being imaginary, simulated, or merely apparent. Frequently used to contrast lived experience with fiction, theory, or digital simulation. | **Core:** real, unreal, reality, unreality<br>**Constructions:** in real life, in the real world, for real, get real, reality check, virtual reality, augmented reality, escape from reality<br>**Derivations:** realize, realization, realism, realistic, unrealistic | **real/reality** overlaps with GROUP 2 (authenticity); **true/truth** overlaps from GROUP 1 | Focus on existence and actuality rather than truth of statements or authenticity of objects. Shows tension between ontological and authenticity senses. |
| GROUP 4: LOGICAL AND ARGUMENTATIVE SOUNDNESS | Terms used to evaluate the logical structure and inferential validity of arguments, reasoning, and claims. These expressions assess whether conclusions follow from premises, whether reasoning is well-founded, or whether arguments contain logical flaws. Primarily used in academic, philosophical, and analytical discourse. | **Core:** valid, invalid, sound, unsound, fallacious, fallacy<br>**Constructions:** spurious correlation, truth value, truth condition<br>**Derivations:** validity, validate, validation, invalidate, soundness, fallibility, infallible | **valid/validity** overlaps with GROUP 8 (legitimacy) and GROUP 11 (technical); **sound** overlaps with GROUP 5 (reliability) | Evaluate logical structure rather than factual content, though distinction often blurs in practice. |
| GROUP 5: RELIABILITY AND DEPENDABILITY | Terms used to evaluate whether sources, persons, instruments, or systems can be consistently depended upon to function properly or provide accurate information. These expressions assess trustworthiness based on track record and consistency rather than single instances. Common in contexts of testimony, mechanical function, and institutional assessment. | **Core:** reliable, unreliable, trustworthy, untrustworthy<br>**Constructions:** safe and sound, tried and reliable<br>**Derivations:** reliability, reliably, trustworthiness, trust, distrust | **sound** overlaps from GROUP 4 | Emphasize consistency and track record rather than single-instance accuracy. |
| GROUP 6: MORAL HONESTY AND TRUTHFULNESS | Terms used to evaluate whether persons habitually tell the truth, act without deception, or represent themselves sincerely. These expressions assess character and moral disposition toward truthfulness rather than accuracy of specific statements. Common in character evaluation and interpersonal trust contexts. | **Core:** honest, dishonest, truthful, untruthful, faithful<br>**Constructions:** to be honest, honest to God, honest broker, honest mistake, bear false witness, faithful to the original<br>**Derivations:** honesty, honestly, dishonesty, truthfulness, faithfulness, unfaithful | **faithful** overlaps with GROUP 9 (precision) | Evaluate character and habitual behavior rather than single statements or objects. Shows range from moral loyalty to representational accuracy. |
| GROUP 7: APPROPRIATENESS AND FITTINGNESS | Terms used to evaluate whether something is suitable, proper, or well-matched to its context, purpose, or circumstances. These expressions assess contextual fit and propriety rather than factual accuracy or authenticity. Common in evaluations of descriptions, responses, behavior, and social conduct. | **Core:** apt, fitting, proper<br>**Constructions:** apt to (do something), it is fitting that, prim and proper<br>**Derivations:** aptly, aptness, aptitude, fittingly, inept, ineptitude | None noted | Evaluate suitability and contextual appropriateness rather than truth or authenticity. |
| GROUP 8: LEGITIMACY AND AUTHORIZATION | Terms used to evaluate whether claims, authority, status, or actions conform to law, rules, or accepted standards of legitimacy. These expressions assess legal or institutional validity and proper authorization rather than factual accuracy. Common in legal, political, and institutional contexts. | **Core:** legitimate, valid (legal sense), bona fide<br>**Constructions:** legitimate concern/question, no longer valid, bona fide offer<br>**Derivations:** validity (legal sense), validate (legal sense), invalidate | **valid/validity** overlaps from GROUP 4 | Focus on legal/institutional status rather than factual truth or logical soundness. |
| GROUP 9: PRECISION AND EXACTNESS | Terms used to evaluate the degree of precision, exactness, or detailed correctness in measurements, representations, or descriptions. These expressions emphasize fine-grained accuracy and attention to detail rather than general correspondence to facts. Common in technical, scientific, and careful descriptive contexts. | **Core:** accurate, inaccurate<br>**Constructions:** accurate to within (X), strictly accurate, right on the money<br>**Derivations:** accuracy, accurately, inaccuracy | **correct/incorrect** overlaps from GROUP 1; **faithful** overlaps from GROUP 6 | Emphasize degree of precision rather than simple truth/falsity. |
| GROUP 10: RIGHTNESS IN MORAL AND PRACTICAL DOMAINS | Terms used to evaluate moral propriety of actions, practical correctness of procedures, or appropriate functioning of situations. These expressions span moral judgment, practical know-how, and situational assessment, often blurring boundaries between ethical and pragmatic evaluation. Extremely common in everyday discourse across multiple domains. | **Core:** right, wrong, correct (procedural sense)<br>**Constructions:** do right by (someone), in the wrong, serve someone right, go wrong, can't go wrong (with X), two wrongs don't make a right, set things right, make it right<br>**Derivations:** rightness, rightful, righteous, righteousness, wrongdoing, wrongful | **right/wrong** overlaps with GROUP 1; **correct** overlaps from GROUP 1; **true/truth** overlaps from GROUP 1 | Operate across moral, practical, and functional domains with fluid boundaries. Show extensive polysemy. |
| GROUP 11: TECHNICAL VERIFICATION AND TESTING | Terms used in technical, scientific, and diagnostic contexts to mark results of testing, verification, or validation procedures. These expressions often appear in specialized collocations related to testing methodology, statistical analysis, and quality control. Common in scientific, medical, and technical discourse. | **Core:** valid (testing sense), invalid (testing sense)<br>**Constructions:** false positive, false negative, false alarm, spurious correlation<br>**Derivations:** validate (technical sense), validation (technical sense), falsifiable, falsification (scientific sense) | **valid/invalid** overlaps from GROUP 4; **false/falsity** overlaps from GROUP 1 | Operate in specialized technical contexts with specific methodological meanings. |
| (Ungrouped Items) | Items that do not fit cleanly into identified groups or show insufficient distinctive patterning. | truism, truthiness, post-truth, half-truth, realpolitik, reality TV, veridical (marginal/technical), veritable (emphatic modifier), so-called (metalinguistic) | None applicable | These items either operate at metalevel (commenting on truth rather than evaluating it), denote types of statements rather than evaluate them, or function as specialized borrowings/neologisms with limited integration into the core semantic system. |

#### F3_semantic_groups_table
# F3 — SEMANTIC GROUPS TABLE

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| Factual Accuracy and Correctness | This group comprises expressions used when assessing whether statements, information, or representations correspond to facts or meet standards of accuracy. These terms appear in contexts of verification, confirmation, and correction, particularly in administrative, educational, and informational discourse. They contrast with terms indicating error or inaccuracy. | ukweli (truth, reality, fact), sahihi (correct, accurate, right, proper, authentic), kweli (true, truth, real, really, indeed), -a kweli (of truth, true, genuine, real), madhubuti (reliable, accurate, precise, firm, trustworthy), thibitisha (to confirm, to verify, to establish, to prove), ushahidi (evidence, testimony, witness, proof), hoja (argument, proof, evidence, reason), dhahiri (clear, evident, obvious, apparent, manifest), hakika (certain, sure, definite, indeed, really), sawa (correct, right, okay, equal, same, appropriate), kamili (complete, perfect, whole, entire, accurate) | kamili overlaps with Group 6 when implying accuracy through completeness; haki overlaps secondarily with this group in its "truth" sense | Typically neutral regarding intention; applies primarily to propositional content (statements, claims, information) |
| Falsehood and Deception | This group includes expressions used to characterize statements, representations, or behaviors as deliberately false or misleading. These terms appear prominently in moral condemnation, accusations of dishonesty, and warnings about deception. They often involve intentionality or moral judgment beyond simple factual incorrectness. | uongo (lie, falsehood, untruth), -a uongo (of falsehood, false, lying, deceptive), mwongo/waongo (liar/liars), -danganya (to deceive, to lie, to trick, to cheat, to mislead), mdanganyifu/wadanganyifu (deceiver/deceivers, liar/liars, trickster/tricksters), udanganyifu (deception, deceitfulness, trickery, dishonesty), bandia (fake, artificial, counterfeit, false, imitation) | bandia appears in both Group 2 (when referring to false representations) and Group 3 (when contrasting with genuine materials); usage context determines which aspect is foregrounded | Strongly implies intentional wrongdoing; applies primarily to propositional content; shows less gradability in practice |

# G1 — Cross-Language Summary of Observed Semantic Organization

## 1. Language Inventory

- **zh (Chinese)** — Large vocabulary with morphologically transparent compounds; extensive use of 真/假/实/正/对/错 root families; rich fixed expressions (chengyu); strong integration of correctness, authenticity, and moral uprightness under shared roots.
- **he (Hebrew)** — Root-and-pattern morphology (binyan system); primary root family א-מ-נ covers truth, reliability, faith, and belief; strong lexical distinction between factual correspondence (אמת/שקר) and justice/rightness (צדק); productive ψευδ- equivalent through שקר compounds.
- **sa (Sanskrit)** — Highly systematic philosophical vocabulary; satya/mithyā/dharma/pramāṇa as core terms; two-truths framework (vyavahāra/paramārtha) prominent; epistemological apparatus (pramāṇa, pramā, bhrama) more elaborated than in other languages.
- **el (Greek)** — Highly productive ψευδ- prefix generating pseudo-X compounds; ορθ- root covers correctness, orthodoxy, and technical domains; αλήθεια family covers truth; strong lexical differentiation between truth-telling, authenticity, correctness, justice, and validity.
- **en (English)** — Large vocabulary with mixed Germanic/Latinate roots; extensive fixed expressions and idioms; strong derivational productivity (false → falsify → falsification → falsifiable); notable gap: no single-word agentive for "truth-teller."
- **tl (Tagalog)** — Circumfix morphology (ka-...-an, pag-, ma-, -in, -an) generates systematic nominal and verbal forms; totoo/tunay distinction (factual truth vs. genuine authenticity) is a notable lexical split; particle system (ba, nga, lang, naman) creates pragmatic constructions.
- **sw (Swahili)** — Noun class system with u- prefix for abstract nouns; heavy Arabic loanword influence (sahihi, hakika, halisi, haki, adili); productive -isha causative and -ika stative suffixes; kweli/uongo as primary opposition.
- **qu (Quechua)** — Agglutinative morphology with obligatory evidential suffixes (-mi, -si, -cha); chiqan/llulla as primary opposition; allin covers broad positive evaluation; no dedicated inchoative for "becoming bad"; evidential system grammatically encodes epistemic stance on truth claims.

## 2. Per-Language Semantic Sketches

### zh (Chinese)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Chinese organizes truth-related vocabulary around four major roots: 真 (genuine/true), 实 (solid/real/actual), 正 (correct/upright), and 对/错 (correct/wrong). These roots overlap substantially: 真实 combines both truth and reality; 正确 combines uprightness and definiteness. The F3 analysis identifies 18 semantic groups, including separate groups for authenticity of objects (Group 1), factual correspondence (Group 2), correctness of answers (Group 3), precision (Group 4), honesty/sincerity (Group 5), deception (Group 6), substantiality (Group 7), practical implementation (Group 8), reliability (Group 9), normality (Group 10), legitimacy (Group 11), consistency between appearance and reality (Group 12), rationality (Group 13), practical utility (Group 14), empirical investigation (Group 15), discourse markers (Group 16), spatial/temporal precision (Group 17), and mathematical/technical terminology (Group 18).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The -性 suffix creates abstract quality nouns and -度 creates measurable degree nouns, both restricted to disyllabic bases. Monosyllabic roots (真, 假, 正) cannot directly take these suffixes. Resultative verb compounds (改正, 落实, 证实) are a distinctive feature where truth-domain roots function as resultative complements. The root 正 is unusually productive as a resultative complement (纠正, 改正, 修正, 端正).

**Constructional patterns (F4):** Bare inchoative patterns (变真, 变假) are marginal; resultative compounds (落实, 坐实, 证实) are strongly preferred for causation of truth-domain states. The 把-disposal construction is standard for correction (把...改正). AABB reduplication (实实在在) is productive for emphasis. Agentive nominalization for "truth-teller" is absent as a productive pattern.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The 真/假 and 实/虚 oppositions are the most productive, generating numerous compound pairs. Fixed expressions frequently embed oppositions internally (真假难辨, 半真半假, 虚虚实实). The 正/不正 opposition is morphological. Many oppositions are constructional, using parallel verb phrases (揭露真相 vs. 隐瞒真相).

---

### he (Hebrew)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** The root א-מ-נ generates a remarkably wide family: אמת (truth), אמין (reliable), נאמן (faithful), אמונה (faith/belief), להאמין (to believe), אמן (amen). This single root covers factual truth, reliability, faith, and belief — domains that are lexically distinct in most other languages in this corpus. The root צ-ד-ק covers both factual rightness (צודק = "you're right") and moral justice (צדק = justice, צדקה = charity). F3 identifies 11 groups including factual correspondence, authenticity, reliability/trustworthiness, honesty/sincerity, justice/moral rightness, belief/faith, validity/logical soundness, precision, certainty, practicality/realism, and discourse management.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The -ut suffix productively creates abstract nouns from adjectives (אמינות, נאמנות, מהימנות). The binyan system creates systematic causative/passive alternations (להצדיק/מוצדק, לזייף/מזויף). The root א-מ-נ shows unusual semantic breadth, appearing across Groups 1, 3, 6, and 11 of F3. The term מוצדק (justified) shows dual moral/logical application, appearing in both Group 5 (justice) and Group 7 (validity).

**Constructional patterns (F4):** Zero copula in present tense is the default. The verb התברר (hitbarer, "it became clear/turned out") is the standard inchoative for truth-revelation, with no direct equivalent in most other languages. Causative constructions for "making true" are absent; instead, Hebrew uses verbs of proving (הוכיח), verifying (אימת), or establishing (ביסס). The metaphor of truth as a hidden object that can be revealed (גילה, חשף, הוציא לאור) or concealed (הסתיר, כיסה) is highly productive.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** אמת/שקר is the primary lexical opposition. Morphological negation with לא is the dominant negation strategy. Several oppositions are scalar rather than binary (קשה להאמין vs. אי אפשר להאמין). The pairing אמת ושלום (truth and peace) represents a culturally specific tension not found in other languages.

---

### sa (Sanskrit)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Sanskrit has the most elaborated epistemological vocabulary in the corpus. The pramāṇa system (perception, inference, testimony as valid knowledge sources) has no parallel in other languages. The satya/mithyā opposition covers both factual truth and ontological reality/illusion. The vyavahāra/paramārtha distinction (conventional vs. ultimate truth) is unique to this corpus. F3 identifies 10 groups: factual correspondence, epistemic validity/justification, cognitive error/illusion, metaphysical falsity/illusoriness, moral truthfulness/deception, righteousness/proper conduct, ignorance/knowledge, Vedic cosmic-moral order (archaic), essential nature/identity, and similarity/correspondence.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The privative prefix a-/an- is highly productive (asatya, adharma, asādhu, avidyā, ayathārtha, apramā), creating systematic antonyms. The -tā and -tva suffixes both create abstract nouns with no clear semantic difference, with lexical preferences varying by base. The dual genitive construction (satyāsatyayoḥ, pramābhramayoḥ) is a distinctive Sanskrit pattern for expressing binary oppositions. The Vedic terms ṛta/anṛta are archaic and largely replaced by satya/asatya in classical usage.

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The ablative standpoint construction (-taḥ suffix: paramārthataḥ, vyavahārataḥ) is unique to Sanskrit in this corpus and marks epistemic/metaphysical perspective. The locative domain construction (vyavahāre satyam, paramārthe satyam) relativizes truth claims to levels of analysis. Causative morphology (NIC suffix) is theoretically available but not attested for truth-domain predicates; causation is expressed periphrastically. The optative mood (brūyāt) is the standard for moral obligation.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The a-/an- privative prefix creates the most systematic set of morphological oppositions in the corpus. The vyavahāra/paramārtha opposition is unique — a scalar/hierarchical rather than binary contrast. The dual construction (satyāsatyayoḥ) embeds opposition within a single grammatical form.

---

### el (Greek)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Greek has the most productive prefix for generating false-X compounds: ψευδ- generates ψευδοεπιστήμη (pseudoscience), ψευδοδημοκρατία (pseudo-democracy), ψευδοπληροφορία (misinformation), and many others. The ορθ- root covers correctness, orthodoxy, and extends into medical (ορθοπεδική), dental (ορθοδοντική), geometric (ορθογώνιο), and linguistic (ορθογραφία) domains. F3 identifies 17 groups including truth-telling/lying, legal/testimonial falsity, authenticity of objects, sincerity/hypocrisy, correctness/error, precision, reality vs. appearance, justice/fairness, legal validity, certainty/doubt, substantiality, pseudo-X constructions, misinformation, orthographic correctness, orthodox belief, technical ορθ- extensions, and rationality.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The -ότητα suffix productively creates abstract nouns from adjectives (αληθινότητα, αυθεντικότητα, εγκυρότητα). The ψευδ- prefix is more productive than equivalents in other languages, generating a distinct semantic group (Group 12) of pseudo-X constructions. There is a notable gap: no single-word agentive for "truth-teller" (*αληθευτής is not standard), while ψεύτης (liar) is fully lexicalized.

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The verb γίνομαι (become) + adjective is the standard inchoative. The verb αποκαλύπτεται (is revealed) is the standard passive for truth-revelation. The verb διαψεύδω (disprove/refute) has no close parallel in other languages. Several discourse markers are grammaticalized from truth terms (αλήθεια? as surprise marker, πραγματικά as "really/basically," ουσιαστικά as "basically"). The construction "expose as fake" (εκθέτω ως ψεύτικο) is well-attested.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The αλήθεια/ψέμα opposition is primary. Color metaphors for lies (άσπρο ψέμα "white lie," μαύρο ψέμα "black lie") are attested. The αληθοφάνεια/αλήθεια (verisimilitude vs. truth) distinction is notable. Several oppositions lack attested lexical counterparts (ορθολογικός lacks an attested opposite in the data; ορθοδοξία lacks an attested heterodoxy term).

---

### en (English)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** English has the largest raw vocabulary in the corpus, with extensive fixed expressions and idioms. The true/false, real/unreal, genuine/fake, correct/incorrect, right/wrong, valid/invalid, honest/dishonest, reliable/unreliable families are all distinct. F3 identifies 11 groups: correspondence to facts, authenticity of objects/credentials, ontological reality vs. appearance, logical/argumentative soundness, reliability/dependability, moral honesty/truthfulness, appropriateness/fittingness, legitimacy/authorization, precision/exactness, rightness in moral/practical domains, and technical verification/testing. The "right/wrong" pair is notably polysemous, spanning epistemic, moral, and practical domains.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The false → falsify → falsification → falsifiable → falsifiability chain is unusually long and productive, reflecting the influence of philosophy of science. The term "truthiness" (coined 2005) and "post-truth" (prominent 2016) are neologisms with no equivalents in other languages in the corpus. The agentive gap for "truth-teller" (no single word; "liar" is fully lexicalized) parallels Greek. The word "right" is the most polysemous truth-domain term in the corpus, covering epistemic correctness, moral propriety, legal entitlement, and practical appropriateness.

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The "come true" construction is restricted to the adjective "true" and does not extend to other truth-domain adjectives (*came false, *came authentic are ungrammatical). Direct causatives like "make X true" are largely ungrammatical; dedicated causative verbs (verify, authenticate, validate, falsify, correct) are required. The "prove X wrong/right" resultative is productive. The "so-called" construction marks metalinguistic skepticism about category membership.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** Morphological negation (un-, in-, dis-) is the dominant strategy for creating antonyms. The false positive/false negative opposition is a technical pair unique to this corpus. The real/surreal and real/virtual reality oppositions reflect modern technological and artistic contexts.

### tl (Tagalog)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Tagalog has a notable lexical split between totoo (factual truth, correspondence to reality) and tunay (genuineness, authenticity, sincerity). This distinction is more grammatically marked than in most other languages. F3 identifies 15 groups including factual correspondence, authenticity/genuineness, correctness/error, deception/lying, cheating/fraud, illusion/deceptive appearance, fabrication/invention, evidence/proof, concealment/revelation, honesty/sincerity, appropriateness/fit, discourse management, emphatic/intensifying constructions, comparative/superlative constructions, and cessation/sufficiency expressions. The last group (tama na = "enough/stop") represents a semantic extension of a correctness term into a cessation domain not found in other languages.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The circumfix ka-...-an productively creates abstract nouns (katotohanan, katunayan, katapatan, katamaan). The pag- prefix creates action nominals. The -in patient voice and -an locative/benefactive suffixes create systematic verbal alternations. The causative pa- + tunay generates patunayan (to prove), with further derivations (mapatunayan, napatunayan, pinatunayan). The tama na construction shows semantic drift from correctness to cessation/sufficiency, which is unique in the corpus.

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The particle system (ba for questions, nga for emphatic affirmation, lang for limitation, naman for concession, pa for continuation) generates a large number of pragmatic constructions from base truth terms. The existential predicates may/walang (has/without) with abstract nouns (may katotohanan, walang katunayan) are a productive pattern for asserting or denying presence of truth/evidence. The ang topic-focus construction (tama ang...) is distinctive.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The totoo/kasinungalingan and tunay/peke oppositions are primary. The may/walang existential opposition is highly productive. The tama/mali opposition is the primary correctness pair. The lantád/lihim (exposed/hidden) opposition is a distinctive revelation/concealment pair.

### sw (Swahili)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Swahili truth vocabulary is heavily influenced by Arabic loanwords: sahihi (correct, from ṣaḥīḥ), hakika (certain, from ḥaqīqa), halisi (genuine, from ḫāliṣ), haki (right/justice, from ḥaqq), adili (just, from ʿādil). The native root kweli/uongo provides the primary truth/falsehood opposition. F3 identifies 9 groups: factual accuracy/correctness, falsehood/deception, genuineness/authenticity, rights/justice/moral correctness, error/deviation, completeness/perfection, clarity/obviousness, certainty/confidence, and purity/cleanliness (extended to truth).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The u- prefix creates abstract nouns (ukweli, uongo, usahihi, uhakika, uhalisia, uadilifu). The -isha causative suffix is highly productive (sahihisha, hakikisha, kamilisha, dhihirisha, safisha). The -ika stative suffix creates intransitive statives (kamilika, hakikika). The noun class system requires agreement across all modifying elements. The Arabic loanwords do not always integrate fully into the derivational system — some (like sahihi) take -isha causatives productively, while others show more limited derivation.

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The copular ni/si (is/is not) is invariant across noun classes, simplifying attribution constructions. The verb-object collocations (sema ukweli, toa ushahidi) are highly conventionalized. The kwa + abstract noun adverbial pattern (kwa kweli, kwa usahihi, kwa hakika) is productive. Reduplication (kweli kweli, sawa sawa) is marginal and primarily informal. The -ish- causative is the primary means of expressing causation of truth-domain states.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The kweli/uongo opposition is primary. The halisi/bandia (genuine/fake) opposition is the main authenticity pair. Several logical opposites are not attested in the data (adili lacks an attested opposite; dhahiri lacks an attested hidden/secret opposite; safi lacks an attested dirty/impure opposite in the truth domain). The ni/si copular alternation is the most productive negation strategy.

### qu (Quechua)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):** Quechua has the most grammatically integrated evidential system in the corpus: the suffixes -mi (direct knowledge), -si (reportative/hearsay), and -cha (conjectural) are obligatory in main clauses and directly encode the epistemic basis of truth claims. The primary opposition is chiqan (true/genuine) vs. llulla (false/lying). The term allin covers broad positive evaluation across moral, practical, and aesthetic domains. F3 identifies 14 groups: truth-asserting terms, falsehood/deception, error/mistake, positive evaluation, negative evaluation, knowledge/epistemic terms, perception/appearance, verification/authentication, completeness/wholeness, existence/being, directness/straightness, emphatic/intensifying particles, speech/communication, and character/disposition.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:** The -ya- inchoative suffix (allinyay = become good) is productive for positive change but no parallel inchoative for "becoming bad" is attested. The -cha- causative (allinchay = make good, chiqanchay = verify) and -ku- reflexive combine productively. The -q agentive nominalizer creates agent nouns (llullakuq = liar). The evidential suffixes attach to truth-domain terms to create epistemically marked assertions (chiqapmi, chiqapsi, chiqapcha). The accusative -ta with truth terms creates the standard "speak the truth/lie" construction (chiqanta rimay, llullata rimay).

**Constructional patterns (F4):** The evidential system is the most distinctive feature: all main-clause assertions about truth are marked for epistemic source. Prohibitive constructions require both ama and -chu (ama llullakychu). Locative and directional constructions with truth terms (chiqanpi kay, chiqanman kutiy) are marginal and metaphorical. The disjunctive question (chiqanchu llullachu = true or false?) is a productive pattern. No simple verb for "becoming bad/false" is attested; periphrastic constructions are required.

**Oppositional structures (F5):** The chiqan/llulla opposition is primary and generates parallel compound pairs (chiqan runa/llulla runa, chiqan simi/llulla simi, chiqan kaq/llulla kaq). The allin/mana allin opposition is morphological (negation). Several expected opposites are absent: no inchoative for deterioration, no causative for making bad, no dedicated antonym for pantay (to err).

## 3. Cross-Language Summary

### Recurring Convergences (patterns observed in many languages)

- **A primary binary opposition between truth and falsehood is present in all eight languages**, typically as a lexical pair: zh 真/假, he אמת/שקר, sa satya/asatya, el αλήθεια/ψέμα, en true/false, tl totoo/kasinungalingan (or totoo/llulla in qu), sw kweli/uongo, qu chiqan/llulla. In all languages, this opposition is the most productive source of derived forms and constructions.

- **A distinction between factual truth (correspondence to reality) and authenticity/genuineness (of objects or persons) is present in most languages**, though the degree of lexical separation varies. Chinese distinguishes 真实 (factual) from 真品/真迹 (authentic objects); Hebrew distinguishes אמת (factual) from אמיתי/אותנטי (genuine); Tagalog has the clearest lexical split (totoo vs. tunay); Swahili distinguishes kweli (truth) from halisi (genuine); Greek distinguishes αλήθεια (truth) from γνήσιος/αυθεντικός (authentic). Sanskrit, English, and Quechua show less sharp lexical separation between these domains.

- **Morphological negation is the dominant strategy for creating antonyms of truth-domain terms in all languages.** Chinese uses 不/非/无, Hebrew uses לא, Sanskrit uses a-/an-, Greek uses α-/αν-, English uses un-/in-/dis-, Tagalog uses hindi/di-, Swahili uses si/mana, Quechua uses mana. In all cases, morphological negation is more productive than dedicated lexical antonyms for most truth-domain terms.

- **Causative constructions for establishing, verifying, or correcting truth are present in all languages**, but the preferred strategy varies: Chinese uses resultative verb compounds (改正, 落实, 证实); Hebrew uses dedicated causative verbs (הוכיח, אימת, ביסס); Sanskrit uses causative morphology (-ish-) and dedicated verbs; Greek uses dedicated verbs (βεβαιώνω, αποδεικνύω, ακυρώνω); English uses dedicated causative verbs (verify, authenticate, validate, falsify, correct); Tagalog uses pa-causative (patunayan); Swahili uses -isha causative (sahihisha, hakikisha); Quechua uses -cha- causative (chiqanchay, allinchay).

- **Discourse markers derived from truth terms are present in all languages.** Chinese: 说真的, 说实话, 老实说; Hebrew: באמת?, להיות כנה; Sanskrit: satyam (as emphatic particle); Greek: αλήθεια? (surprise), πραγματικά (really/basically); English: to be honest, to tell the truth; Tagalog: sa totoo lang, totoo lang; Swahili: kwa kweli, kwa hakika; Quechua: chiqap, k'ari. In all languages, these forms have undergone some degree of pragmatic grammaticalization beyond their literal truth-evaluating function.

- **A gap in agentive nominalization for "truth-teller" (as opposed to "liar") is observable in multiple languages.** English lacks a single-word equivalent (*truth-teller is a compound, not a derived form); Greek lacks *αληθευτής; Chinese lacks a productive single-word form. By contrast, "liar" is lexicalized in all languages: zh 说谎者/骗子, he שקרן, sa mithyāvādin, el ψεύτης, en liar, tl sinungaling, sw mwongo, qu llullakuq. This asymmetry — liar is lexicalized, truth-teller is not — appears across at least five of the eight languages.

- **Constructions treating truth as a hidden object that can be revealed or concealed are attested in multiple languages.** Hebrew: האמת תצא לאור (truth will come to light), הסתיר את האמת (hide the truth); Greek: βγαίνει η αλήθεια στη φόρα (truth comes to the surface), κρύβω την αλήθεια; English: the truth came to light, hide the truth; Tagalog: lantád/lihim (exposed/hidden); Swahili: gundua ukweli (discover truth), ficha ukweli (hide truth). This spatial/container metaphor for truth is absent or marginal in Sanskrit and Quechua.

---

### Major Divergences (patterns observed in only one or two languages)

- **Sanskrit alone has a fully elaborated epistemological apparatus as part of the core truth vocabulary.** The pramāṇa system (perception, inference, testimony as distinct valid knowledge sources), the pramā/apramā/bhrama distinctions, and the vyavahāra/paramārtha two-truths framework have no parallels in the other seven languages. Other languages have epistemic vocabulary (Hebrew ודאי, English valid, Quechua yachay), but none organizes it into a systematic epistemological taxonomy within the truth-domain vocabulary.

- **Quechua alone has grammatically obligatory evidential marking on truth-domain assertions.** The suffixes -mi (direct knowledge), -si (hearsay), and -cha (conjecture) are not optional emphatic particles but grammatical requirements in main clauses. This means that in Quechua, every assertion about truth is grammatically marked for its epistemic source, a feature absent in all other languages in the corpus.

- **Greek alone has a highly productive ψευδ- prefix generating a distinct semantic group of "pseudo-X" constructions** (ψευδοεπιστήμη, ψευδοδημοκρατία, ψευδοδιανοούμενος, etc.). While other languages have some equivalent compounds (English pseudo-science, Chinese 伪科学), none generates them as systematically from a single prefix that is also the root for "lie/false."

- **Tagalog alone shows a semantic extension of a correctness term (tama) into a cessation/sufficiency domain** (tama na = "enough/stop"). This semantic drift, where a term meaning "correct" comes to mean "sufficient" or "stop," is not attested in the other seven languages.

- **Sanskrit and Chinese alone have a formally marked two-level or hierarchical truth distinction.** Sanskrit has vyavahāra (conventional) vs. paramārtha (ultimate), with dedicated adverbial forms (vyavahārataḥ, paramārthataḥ). Chinese has 实际 (practical/actual) vs. 本质 (essential nature) and the philosophical 真理 (fundamental truth) vs. 真相 (factual truth), though less formally marked than Sanskrit. No other language in the corpus has a grammatically marked distinction between levels of truth.

- **Swahili alone shows a large-scale Arabic loanword stratum as the primary source of precision/correctness vocabulary.** While other languages have loanwords (Greek αυθεντικός from Greek into other languages; English bona fide from Latin; Tagalog sinsero from Spanish), Swahili's core truth vocabulary — sahihi, hakika, halisi, haki, adili — is predominantly Arabic-derived, creating a situation where the native root (kweli/uongo) and the Arabic-derived terms (sahihi, hakika) coexist with partially overlapping functions.

- **Hebrew alone has a single root (א-מ-נ) that covers factual truth, reliability, faith, and belief as a unified family.** In all other languages, these domains are covered by distinct roots: Chinese 真 (truth) vs. 信 (belief/trust); Sanskrit satya (truth) vs. śraddhā (faith); Greek αλήθεια (truth) vs. πίστη (faith); English true vs. believe/trust; Tagalog totoo (truth) vs. paniniwala (belief); Swahili kweli (truth) vs. imani (faith); Quechua chiqan (truth) vs. yachay (knowledge). The semantic unity of the א-מ-נ root in Hebrew is a distinctive feature.

---

### Asymmetries, Gaps, and Irregularities

- **The inchoative asymmetry (becoming true/good is lexicalized; becoming false/bad is not) appears in multiple languages.** Quechua has allinyay (become good) but no attested *llullayay (become false) as a pure inchoative. Chinese has 变得真实 (become authentic) but 变假 is marginal. Greek has γίνομαι αληθινός (become true) but the reverse is less natural. English "come true" is restricted to the positive direction (*come false is ungrammatical). This asymmetry — positive change is more readily lexicalized than negative change — appears across at least four languages.

- **The causative asymmetry (making true/correct is lexicalized; making false is often periphrastic or restricted) appears in multiple languages.** English "make X true" is largely ungrammatical; dedicated verbs (verify, authenticate) are required for the positive direction, while falsify covers the negative. Hebrew has no common direct causative "to make X true." Greek lacks a simple causative for making true. Quechua chiqanchay (verify/authenticate) is attested but *llullachay (make false) is not. The negative causative (making false) tends to be expressed through deception verbs (deceive, forge, falsify) rather than through direct causatives of the falsity adjective.

- **Technical/specialized extensions of truth-domain roots into non-truth domains are present in all languages but vary in productivity.** Chinese 正 extends into mathematics (正数, 正比), geometry (正方形), and time (正午, 正点). Greek ορθ- extends into medicine (ορθοπεδική, ορθοδοντική), geometry (ορθογώνιο), and biology (ορθόπτερα). Sanskrit √mā extends into measurement (māna, mātrā, parimāṇa) and construction (nirmāṇa). English false extends into music (falsetto), statistics (false positive/negative), and law (false imprisonment). These extensions are language-specific and do not show cross-linguistic parallelism in their target domains.

- **The relationship between truth and justice/moral rightness is handled differently across languages.** Hebrew צדק (justice/rightness) and צודק (you're right) are from the same root, tightly linking factual correctness with moral justice. Chinese 正 covers both correctness and moral uprightness. Sanskrit dharma covers moral rightness but is distinct from satya (truth). Greek δίκαιος (just) is separate from αληθινός (true). English right covers both but as polysemy rather than derivational unity. Swahili haki covers both truth and rights/justice. Quechua allin covers goodness/correctness but not justice specifically. The degree of lexical integration between truth and justice varies from tight (Hebrew, Chinese) to loose (Sanskrit, Greek, English).

- **Fixed expressions and proverbs about truth and lies are present in all languages but are not cross-linguistically parallel in content.** Chinese has 真金不怕火炼 (true gold fears no fire); Hebrew has האמת תצא לאור (truth will come to light); Greek has το ψέμα έχει κοντά ποδάρια (lies have short legs); English has the truth will out; Tagalog has no single dominant proverb but has the tunay na kulay (true colors) idiom; Swahili has ukweli mtupu (bare truth) as a fixed phrase; Sanskrit has satyam eva jayate (truth alone conquers); Quechua has no proverbs attested in the data. The content of these fixed expressions is not shared across languages, though the existence of such expressions is universal in the corpus.

- **The treatment of "appearance vs. reality" as a distinct semantic domain varies considerably.** Sanskrit has the most elaborate vocabulary for this distinction (mithyā, ābhāsa, vyavahāra/paramārtha, māyā). Greek has αληθοφάνεια (verisimilitude) and εικονικός (virtual/apparent). Chinese has 表里如一 (same inside and out) and 名副其实 (worthy of the name). Hebrew has מציאותי (realistic) and מזויף (forged). English has real/unreal, virtual reality, surreal. Tagalog has palabás (pretense/facade) and kunwari (pretend). Swahili has uhalisia (authenticity/reality). Quechua has rikch'ay/rikch'akuy (to appear/seem). The appearance/reality distinction is present in all languages but is most elaborated in Sanskrit and least elaborated in Quechua.

- **Several languages show productive constructions that are absent or marginal in others.** The Sanskrit dual genitive (satyāsatyayoḥ) for expressing binary oppositions has no parallel. The Tagalog existential may/walang + abstract noun (may katotohanan, walang katunayan) as a truth-assertion strategy has no close parallel. The Quechua evidential suffixes on truth terms have no parallel. The Chinese resultative verb compounds (改正, 落实, 证实) where truth-domain roots function as resultative complements have no parallel. These constructions are each unique to their respective languages in the corpus.

## Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Partition Patterns

**The factual truth/falsity opposition is universal.** Every language in the corpus maintains a primary lexical opposition between truth and falsehood as applied to statements: zh 真/假, he אמת/שקר, sa satya/asatya, el αλήθεια/ψέμα, en true/false, tl totoo/kasinungalingan, sw kweli/uongo, qu chiqan/llulla. This opposition is the most productive source of derived forms and constructions in every language. It is also the most consistently binary: in all eight languages, the primary truth/falsity pair is treated as a direct opposition rather than a scalar or graded contrast.

**A distinction between factual truth and object authenticity is present in most languages, but the degree of lexical separation varies considerably.** At one extreme, Tagalog has the clearest split: totoo is used for factual correspondence of statements, while tunay is used for genuineness and authenticity of persons, objects, and emotions. These two terms are not interchangeable in most contexts. At the other extreme, Quechua uses chiqan for both factual truth and object authenticity without a dedicated split. Chinese, Hebrew, Greek, English, and Swahili fall between these poles: they have specialized terms for object authenticity (zh 真品/真迹, he אמיתי/אותנטי, el γνήσιος/αυθεντικός, en genuine/authentic, sw halisi) that are distinct from the primary truth/falsity terms, but the primary terms (真, אמת, αλήθεια, true, kweli) can also be applied to objects in many contexts. Sanskrit has the least developed vocabulary for object authenticity as a commercial or material domain, with no specialized terms equivalent to zh 真品 or el γνήσιος.

**A correctness/error distinction for answers, procedures, and actions is present in all languages**, but the degree to which it is lexically separated from the factual truth/falsity distinction varies. Chinese maintains a clear separation: 对/错 (correct/wrong) is the primary pair for answers and judgments, while 真/假 is the primary pair for factual truth and object authenticity. Greek similarly separates σωστός/λάθος (correct/wrong) from αλήθεια/ψέμα (truth/lie). Hebrew uses נכון (correct) for factual and procedural correctness, distinct from אמת (truth). Tagalog separates tama/mali (correct/wrong) from totoo/kasinungalingan (true/lie). By contrast, Quechua uses chiqan for both factual truth and correctness without a dedicated correctness/error pair, and allin/mana allin covers both goodness and correctness. Sanskrit uses samyak (right/correct) and sādhu (good/proper) for correctness, but these overlap substantially with moral rightness.

**A moral honesty/sincerity grouping, distinct from factual truth, is present in all languages.** Chinese has 诚/诚实/真诚 (sincere/honest/genuine); Hebrew has כנה/יושר (honest/integrity); Sanskrit has satyavādin/satyavrata (truth-speaking/committed to truth); Greek has ειλικρινής/υποκριτής (sincere/hypocrite); English has honest/dishonest/truthful; Tagalog has tapat/katapatan (honest/honesty); Swahili has adili/uadilifu (just/justice) and the associative construction mtu wa kweli (genuine person); Quechua has chiqan runa/llulla runa (truthful person/lying person) and chiqan sunqu (true heart). In all languages, this grouping evaluates the disposition of persons toward truth-telling rather than the truth-value of specific statements. However, the degree to which this grouping is lexically distinct from the factual truth grouping varies: in Hebrew, the same root (א-מ-נ) covers both; in Chinese, 诚 is clearly distinct from 真; in Tagalog, tapat is clearly distinct from totoo.

**Discourse markers derived from truth terms are present in all languages**, and in all cases these forms have undergone some degree of pragmatic grammaticalization. Chinese 说真的 and 说实话 introduce frank statements; Hebrew באמת? expresses surprise; Greek αλήθεια? functions as a surprise marker; English "to be honest" frames admissions; Tagalog sa totoo lang introduces candid remarks; Swahili kwa kweli emphasizes sincerity; Quechua chiqap and k'ari function as emphatic particles. The cross-linguistic consistency of this pattern — truth terms being recruited as discourse management devices — is notable, though the specific forms and their degree of grammaticalization differ.

**Morphological negation is the dominant antonym-forming strategy in all languages.** No language relies primarily on dedicated lexical antonyms for truth-domain terms; instead, all use some form of negation prefix or particle: zh 不/非/无, he לא, sa a-/an-, el α-/αν-, en un-/in-/dis-, tl hindi/di-, sw si/mana, qu mana. The productivity of this strategy varies: Sanskrit's a-/an- privative is the most systematic, generating asatya, adharma, asādhu, avidyā, ayathārtha, apramā as fully lexicalized forms. English's un-/in-/dis- generates a large number of forms but with some lexical restrictions (dishonest is standard; *undishonest is not). Quechua's mana is a free particle rather than a bound morpheme, making it the most transparent negation strategy.

---

### Where Languages Split More Finely

**Sanskrit splits the epistemic domain most finely.** No other language in the corpus distinguishes pramāṇa (valid means of knowledge), pramā (valid cognition), apramā (invalid cognition), bhrama (error/illusion), bhrānti (confusion/error), and viparyaya (reversal/mistaken cognition) as distinct lexical items. Other languages have epistemic vocabulary, but none organizes it into a systematic taxonomy within the truth-domain vocabulary. Sanskrit also uniquely splits the reality domain into vyavahāra (conventional/empirical reality) and paramārtha (ultimate reality), with dedicated adverbial forms for each level.

**Greek splits the "false" domain most finely through the ψευδ- prefix.** While other languages have some compound-forming capacity with falsity roots, Greek generates a distinct semantic group of pseudo-X constructions (ψευδοεπιστήμη, ψευδοδημοκρατία, ψευδοδιανοούμενος, ψευδοπληροφορία) that is more productive and systematic than any equivalent in the corpus. Greek also splits the legal/testimonial falsity domain more finely than other languages, with dedicated terms for perjury (ψευδορκία), false witness (ψευδομαρτυρία), and false attribution of authorship (ψευδεπίγραφος).

**Tagalog splits the truth/authenticity domain most clearly** through the totoo/tunay distinction. While other languages have separate terms for factual truth and object authenticity, Tagalog's split is more grammatically consistent: totoo is used for factual correspondence, tunay for genuineness and sincerity, and these terms are not freely interchangeable. Tagalog also splits the deception domain more finely than most languages, with separate terms for lying in speech (sinungaling/kasinungalingan), cheating in transactions/games (dáyà), deceptive appearances (linlang), and fabrication/invention (kathâ/gawâ-gawâ).

**Chinese splits the correctness domain most finely** through the 正 root family, which generates separate groupings for correctness of answers (正确), moral uprightness (正直/正派), legitimacy/authority (正当/正统), normality/regularity (正常/正规), and spatial/temporal precision (正中/正午/正点). No other language generates this many distinct sub-groupings from a single correctness root.

---

### Where Languages Merge Distinctions

**Hebrew merges factual truth, reliability, faithfulness, and belief under the א-מ-נ root.** This is the most striking merger in the corpus. In all other languages, these domains are covered by distinct roots: Chinese 真 (truth) vs. 信 (belief/trust); Sanskrit satya (truth) vs. śraddhā (faith); Greek αλήθεια (truth) vs. πίστη (faith); English true vs. believe/trust; Tagalog totoo (truth) vs. paniniwala (belief); Swahili kweli (truth) vs. imani (faith); Quechua chiqan (truth) vs. yachay (knowledge). The semantic unity of the א-מ-נ root in Hebrew means that terms for "reliable source" (מקור אמין), "faithful person" (נאמן), "I believe" (אני מאמין), and "truth" (אמת) all share a common root, creating a lexical network that links epistemic, relational, and religious domains in a way not found elsewhere.

**English merges factual correctness, moral propriety, legal entitlement, and practical appropriateness under "right."** This is the broadest single-term merger in the corpus. "Right" can mean "the answer is right" (factual), "it's the right thing to do" (moral), "it's your right" (legal entitlement), and "the right tool for the job" (practical fit). No other language in the corpus has a single term with this range of application. Chinese 正 is broad but does not cover legal entitlement; Hebrew צדק covers justice and rightness but not practical fit; Quechua allin covers goodness and correctness but not legal entitlement.

**Quechua merges moral goodness, practical correctness, and aesthetic quality under allin.** While other languages have broad positive evaluation terms (Chinese 好, English good), Quechua's allin is distinctive in that it is the primary term for correctness in the truth domain as well as for goodness in the moral domain. The negated form mana allin is the standard expression for "bad/wrong" across all these domains. This merger means that Quechua does not maintain a sharp lexical distinction between "this answer is correct" and "this action is good" — both are expressed through allin/mana allin.

**Swahili merges "right/entitlement" with "truth/justice" under haki** (from Arabic ḥaqq). This term covers both "it is true" (in some contexts) and "it is your right" (legal entitlement), paralleling the Hebrew צדק merger of factual rightness and moral justice, though through a different semantic path (Arabic loanword vs. native root).

**Chinese merges substantiality, actuality, and practical implementation under 实.** The root 实 covers "solid/real" (实体, 实物), "actual/factual" (事实, 实际), "practical implementation" (实施, 实现, 落实), and "honest/sincere" (实话, 老实). This range of application — from ontological reality to practical action to moral character — is broader than any equivalent root in the other languages.

---

### Cases Where a Language Lacks a Clear Lexical Contrast Found Elsewhere

**The appearance/ultimate-reality philosophical distinction is present only in Sanskrit and, to a lesser degree, Chinese.** Sanskrit's vyavahāra/paramārtha distinction, with dedicated adverbial forms (vyavahārataḥ, paramārthataḥ), has no parallel in the other six languages. Chinese has 实际 (practical/actual) vs. 本质 (essential nature) and the philosophical 真理 (fundamental truth) vs. 真相 (factual truth), but these are less formally marked. The other six languages handle this domain through general vocabulary (real/apparent, genuine/fake) without dedicated philosophical terminology.

**A grammatically obligatory evidential system marking epistemic source on truth claims is present only in Quechua.** The suffixes -mi (direct knowledge), -si (hearsay), and -cha (conjecture) are grammatical requirements in main clauses, not optional emphatic particles. All other languages in the corpus have optional epistemic markers (Hebrew ודאי, Chinese 确实, English "apparently," Swahili kwa hakika), but none makes epistemic source grammatically obligatory. This means that in Quechua, the distinction between "I know this directly" and "I heard this from someone" is encoded in the grammar of every truth-related assertion, while in other languages this distinction is expressed only when the speaker chooses to mark it.

**A productive pseudo-X compound system is present only in Greek.** While other languages have some equivalent compounds (English pseudoscience, Chinese 伪科学, Sanskrit pramāṇābhāsa), none generates them as systematically from a single prefix that is also the root for "lie/false." The Greek ψευδ- prefix generates a distinct semantic group of constructions that evaluate whether something falsely claims membership in a legitimate category (science, democracy, philosophy, art). This evaluative function — assessing false claims to category membership — is not lexically systematized in the other seven languages.

**A cessation/sufficiency extension of a correctness term is present only in Tagalog.** The semantic drift of tama (correct) into tama na (enough/stop) is not attested in any other language in the corpus. Chinese 够了 (enough) and 停 (stop) are distinct from correctness terms; Hebrew מספיק (enough) is distinct from נכון (correct); English "that's enough" is distinct from "that's right." The Tagalog merger of correctness and sufficiency/cessation under tama appears to be a language-specific development.

**A dedicated agentive nominalization for "truth-teller" is absent in at least five languages.** English lacks a single derived word (*truth-teller is a compound); Greek lacks *αληθευτής; Chinese lacks a productive single-word form; Swahili lacks a dedicated agent noun for truth-telling (mwenye ukweli is a possessive construction, not an agentive nominalization); Quechua's chiqan rimaq (truth-speaker) is a compound rather than a derived form. By contrast, "liar" is lexicalized in all eight languages: zh 说谎者/骗子, he שקרן, sa mithyāvādin, el ψεύτης, en liar, tl sinungaling, sw mwongo, qu llullakuq. This asymmetry — liar is lexicalized while truth-teller is not — is one of the most consistent cross-linguistic patterns in the corpus.

**A dedicated inchoative for "becoming false/bad" is absent in at least four languages.** Quechua has allinyay (become good) but no attested parallel for deterioration. Chinese 变假 (become fake) is marginal; the preferred expression is 变得虚假. English "come true" is restricted to the positive direction (*come false is ungrammatical). Greek γίνομαι αληθινός (become true) is more natural than the reverse. Hebrew התברר (it became clear/turned out) is the standard inchoative for truth-revelation, but no parallel form for "becoming false" is attested. This asymmetry — positive change toward truth/goodness is more readily lexicalized than negative change — appears across multiple languages, though it is most clearly documented in Quechua and English.

### Distinguishing Well-Attested Cross-Language Patterns from Single-Language Observations

**Well-attested across multiple languages (five or more):**
- Primary binary truth/falsity lexical opposition
- Morphological negation as dominant antonym-forming strategy
- Discourse markers derived from truth terms
- Asymmetry between lexicalized "liar" and non-lexicalized "truth-teller"
- Distinction between factual truth and object authenticity (though degree of lexical separation varies)
- Causative constructions for verification/correction using dedicated verbs rather than direct causatives of truth adjectives
- Constructions treating truth as a hidden object that can be revealed or concealed (attested in he, el, en, tl, sw; absent or marginal in sa and qu)

**Attested in two to four languages:**
- Inchoative asymmetry (becoming true/good more lexicalized than becoming false/bad): qu, en, el, he
- Merger of factual rightness with moral justice under one root: he (צדק), zh (正), sw (haki)
- Broad positive evaluation term covering moral, practical, and epistemic domains: qu (allin), zh (好/allin-like coverage through 正), en (right, partially)
- Technical/specialized extensions of truth-domain roots into non-truth domains: zh (正 → mathematics, geometry, time), el (ορθ- → medicine, geometry, biology), en (false → music, statistics, law), sa (√mā → measurement, construction)

**Single-language observations:**
- Sanskrit's pramāṇa epistemological apparatus
- Quechua's obligatory evidential system on truth claims
- Greek's productive ψευδ- pseudo-X compound system
- Tagalog's tama na cessation/sufficiency extension
- Hebrew's א-מ-נ root merging truth, reliability, faithfulness, and belief
- Sanskrit's vyavahāra/paramārtha two-truths distinction with dedicated adverbial forms
- Swahili's Arabic loanword stratum as primary source of precision/correctness vocabulary
- Chinese's 实 root merging substantiality, actuality, and practical implementation

#### F3_semantic_groups_table
# F3 — SEMANTIC GROUPS TABLE
# Language: Hebrew (he)

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| GROUP 1: Factual Correspondence Terms | This group contains expressions used to evaluate whether statements, claims, or representations correspond to actual states of affairs. These terms are primarily used in contexts of verification, correction, and factual assessment. They focus on the relationship between what is said or represented and what is the case, rather than on moral qualities or personal sincerity. | אמת (emet) "truth" - used for factual accuracy; נכון (nakhon) "correct, right" - standard confirmation of factual correctness; שקר (sheker) "falsehood, lie" - indicates non-correspondence with facts; ברור (barur) "clear, obvious" - indicates manifest factual clarity; מוכח (mukhaḥ) "proven, demonstrated" - indicates established factual status; מדויק (meduyak) "precise, exact" - emphasizes fine-grained factual accuracy; זה נכון (ze nakhon) "that's correct"; לא נכון (lo nakhon) "not correct"; זה שקר (ze sheker) "this is a lie"; עובדה מוכחת (uvda mukhaḥat) "proven fact" | צודק (tsodek) "right, correct" - overlaps with this group in factual contexts but also belongs to Group 3 (moral/justice domain); אמיתי (amiti) "true, genuine" - overlaps with Group 2 (authenticity) but also used for factual truth | ברור (barur) also appears in Group 9 (epistemic certainty) and Group 11 (discourse management); שקר (sheker) also appears in Group 4 (dishonesty) with both factual and moral dimensions |
| GROUP 2: Authenticity and Genuineness Terms | This group contains expressions used to distinguish genuine, original, or real entities from fake, counterfeit, or imitation ones. These terms are commonly applied to objects, artworks, materials, and personal identity, focusing on whether something is what it purports to be rather than on propositional truth. The contrast is typically between authentic/real versus fake/artificial. | אמיתי (amiti) "true, genuine, real" - primary term for genuineness; אותנטי (otenti) "authentic" - emphasizes originality and genuineness; מזויף (mezuyaf) "forged, fake" - indicates deliberate falsification; מציאותי (metsi'uti) "real, realistic" - indicates reality versus imagination; דומה (dome) "similar, resembling" - used in comparisons of genuineness; זה אמיתי (ze amiti) "this is real"; לא אמיתי (lo amiti) "not real, fake"; זה מזויף (ze mezuyaf) "this is fake"; כסף מזויף (kesef mezuyaf) "counterfeit money"; סיפור אמיתי (sipur amiti) "true story" | אמת (emet) "truth" - primarily in Group 1 but appears in constructions emphasizing genuineness (e.g., אמת לאמיתה "absolute truth"); תעודה מזויפת (te'uda mezuyefet) "forged document" - involves both factual falsity and material forgery | דומה (dome) is marginal to this group, primarily a comparison term used in authenticity contexts but not itself an authenticity term; מציאותי (metsi'uti) also appears in Group 10 (practicality) with different aspects of "real" |
| GROUP 3: Reliability and Trustworthiness Terms | This group contains expressions used to assess whether persons, sources, or information can be relied upon or trusted. These terms focus on dependability and credibility rather than immediate factual accuracy, often involving judgments about character, consistency, or institutional authority. They are common in contexts of testimony, information evaluation, and personal relationships. | אמין (amin) "reliable, trustworthy"; נאמן (ne'eman) "faithful, loyal, reliable"; מהימן (meheyman) "reliable, credible"; אמינות (aminut) "reliability, credibility"; נאמנות (ne'emanut) "faithfulness, loyalty"; מהימנות (meheymanut) "reliability, credibility"; מקור אמין (makor amin) "reliable source"; עד מהימן (ed meheyman) "credible witness"; אדם אמין (adam amin) "reliable person"; נאמן לדבריו (ne'eman lidvarav) "true to one's word" | אמת (emet) in constructions like להעיד עדות אמת (leha'id edut emet) "to give true testimony" - involves both factual truth and reliability; נאמן למטרה (ne'eman lamatara) "faithful to the cause" - overlaps with loyalty/commitment contexts | Terms from root א-מ-נ appear across Groups 1, 3, 6, and 11, showing semantic diversification within a single root family |
| GROUP 4: Honesty and Sincerity Terms | This group contains expressions used to evaluate the sincerity and honesty of speakers or actors, focusing on whether they are being truthful in their intentions and communications rather than on the factual accuracy of their statements. These terms emphasize the moral quality of straightforwardness and the absence of deception in personal conduct and speech. | כנה (kene) "honest, sincere"; יושר (yosher) "honesty, integrity, uprightness"; שקרן (shakran) "liar, habitual liar"; שקרנות (shakranut) "lying, mendacity"; להיות כנה (lihyot kene) "to be honest"; בכנות (bikhnut) "honestly, in honesty"; ביושר (beyosher) "honestly, with integrity"; לנהוג ביושר (linhog beyosher) "to act with integrity"; תשובה כנה (tshuva kena) "honest answer" | שקר (sheker) "falsehood, lie" - primarily in Group 1 but also used for moral condemnation of dishonesty; לשקר (leshaker) "to lie" - involves both factual falsity and moral dishonesty; דובר שקרים (dover shkarim) "speaker of lies" - character judgment overlapping with moral assessment | Several terms show movement from literal truth-evaluation to discourse-marking functions (Group 11), including להיות כנה (lihyot kene) used as discourse marker |

#### F3_semantic_groups_table
# CLCA Protocol v3.2 — F3 SEMANTIC GROUPS TABLE
# Language: English (en)

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|-------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| GROUP 1: CORRESPONDENCE TO FACTS | Terms used to evaluate whether statements, beliefs, or representations correspond to actual facts or reality. These expressions are primarily applied to propositions, claims, and assertions, marking whether they accurately describe the world. Commonly used in contexts of verification, fact-checking, and epistemic evaluation. | **Core:** true, false, correct, incorrect, right, wrong, accurate, inaccurate, erroneous<br>**Constructions:** the truth of the matter, get it right/wrong, prove false, hold true | **true/truth** spans GROUP 1, 10, 3; **false/falsity** spans GROUP 1, 2, 11; **correct/incorrect** spans GROUP 1, 10, 9; **right/wrong** spans GROUP 1, 10 | Focus on propositional content rather than objects or persons. Regularly contrasted in verification contexts. |
| GROUP 2: AUTHENTICITY OF OBJECTS AND CREDENTIALS | Terms used to distinguish genuine articles, documents, or credentials from counterfeits, imitations, or fraudulent versions. These expressions evaluate whether physical objects, artworks, documents, or credentials are what they purport to be, focusing on origin, authorship, and legitimacy rather than abstract truth. Common in commercial, legal, and art contexts. | **Core:** genuine, authentic, fake, counterfeit, bogus, spurious<br>**Constructions:** the genuine article, the real McCoy, the real deal, fake it till you make it, spot a fake, under false pretenses<br>**Derivations:** authenticate, authentication, counterfeit (verb), fakery | **false/falsity** overlaps from GROUP 1; **real/reality** overlaps from GROUP 3; **bogus** shows limited integration | Apply to tangible objects and documents rather than abstract propositions. |
| GROUP 3: ONTOLOGICAL REALITY VS. APPEARANCE | Terms that distinguish actual existence or substance from appearance, simulation, imagination, or virtuality. These expressions mark whether something exists in the physical/actual world versus being imaginary, simulated, or merely apparent. Frequently used to contrast lived experience with fiction, theory, or digital simulation. | **Core:** real, unreal, reality, unreality<br>**Constructions:** in real life, in the real world, for real, get real, reality check, virtual reality, augmented reality, escape from reality<br>**Derivations:** realize, realization, realism, realistic, unrealistic | **real/reality** overlaps with GROUP 2 (authenticity); **true/truth** overlaps from GROUP 1 | Focus on existence and actuality rather than truth of statements or authenticity of objects. Shows tension between ontological and authenticity senses. |
| GROUP 4: LOGICAL AND ARGUMENTATIVE SOUNDNESS | Terms used to evaluate the logical structure and inferential validity of arguments, reasoning, and claims. These expressions assess whether conclusions follow from premises, whether reasoning is well-founded, or whether arguments contain logical flaws. Primarily used in academic, philosophical, and analytical discourse. | **Core:** valid, invalid, sound, unsound, fallacious, fallacy<br>**Constructions:** spurious correlation, truth value, truth condition<br>**Derivations:** validity, validate, validation, invalidate, soundness, fallibility, infallible | **valid/validity** overlaps with GROUP 8 (legitimacy) and GROUP 11 (technical); **sound** overlaps with GROUP 5 (reliability) | Evaluate logical structure rather than factual content, though distinction often blurs in practice. |
| GROUP 5: RELIABILITY AND DEPENDABILITY | Terms used to evaluate whether sources, persons, instruments, or systems can be consistently depended upon to function properly or provide accurate information. These expressions assess trustworthiness based on track record and consistency rather than single instances. Common in contexts of testimony, mechanical function, and institutional assessment. | **Core:** reliable, unreliable, trustworthy, untrustworthy<br>**Constructions:** safe and sound, tried and reliable<br>**Derivations:** reliability, reliably, trustworthiness, trust, distrust | **sound** overlaps from GROUP 4 | Emphasize consistency and track record rather than single-instance accuracy. |
| GROUP 6: MORAL HONESTY AND TRUTHFULNESS | Terms used to evaluate whether persons habitually tell the truth, act without deception, or represent themselves sincerely. These expressions assess character and moral disposition toward truthfulness rather than accuracy of specific statements. Common in character evaluation and interpersonal trust contexts. | **Core:** honest, dishonest, truthful, untruthful, faithful<br>**Constructions:** to be honest, honest to God, honest broker, honest mistake, bear false witness, faithful to the original<br>**Derivations:** honesty, honestly, dishonesty, truthfulness, faithfulness, unfaithful | **faithful** overlaps with GROUP 9 (precision) | Evaluate character and habitual behavior rather than single statements or objects. Shows range from moral loyalty to representational accuracy. |
